title: Mission Control becomes the operating surface
dek: A week of shipping turned Mission Control from a shell into the place where studio work, signals, metrics, design, and preferences meet.
body:
The first version of Mission Control was deliberately modest: a persistent shell with places for the studio's active work, saved signals, and flow metrics. That sounds like navigation, but the important part was ownership. Once the shell existed, the question changed from 'where does this view live?' to 'what operating loop should be visible here?'

## From tabs to an operating surface

The shell MVP gave SIndustries a single place to gather the loops that were already running. Task work had state. Saved signals had review status. Delivery had enough history to show flow metrics. The design system had tokens and components. Each part was useful on its own, but the work still felt split across surfaces. Mission Control became the container for joining them without pretending they were one product yet.

The saved-signal tab was the first real proof. Instead of treating bookmarks as a background pipeline, Mission Control made the review state visible: KPIs, topic breakdowns, pending approvals, and recent transitions. That changed the feel of the workflow. A saved signal was no longer just something an agent might process later. It became an item moving through an observable system.

## The shell starts carrying product behaviour

The next shift was theme ownership. Day/night mode moved into the shell and synchronised across the workspace, including embedded task views. That is a small feature with a bigger implication: Mission Control is not only a menu around other tools. It can own shared behaviour that every operating surface should inherit.

That matters because internal tools usually decay in two directions. Either every workflow grows its own small UI until the studio has a pile of disconnected dashboards, or a central dashboard becomes decorative and never earns daily use. Mission Control is trying to take the third path: one shell, many specialised loops, shared state where it helps, and enough visibility that handoffs become easier to trust.

## Why this week matters

The week-long arc is the useful signal. First came the shell. Then the saved-signal view made an existing pipeline legible. Then design-system access and shell-owned preferences made the workspace feel like one environment instead of several embedded tools. None of those ships is the whole product by itself. Together, they describe a pattern: turn the studio's internal operating loops into visible, shared surfaces, then let the surface reveal what should be productised next.

Mission Control is still early. Its value is not that it has every tab. Its value is that the tabs are starting to describe how SIndustries actually works: capture signal, decide what matters, move work through delivery, watch the flow, and keep the system coherent while it changes.

## Scheduling becomes part of the surface

Content Scheduler extended the shell from observation into action. Approved posts can now be composed, scheduled, and published from the same place the underlying work is reviewed. A ten-day calendar makes that queue visible and lets a post move to a new day without rebuilding the campaign. Publication still passes through explicit approval and cadence gates; the shell removes coordination work without removing judgment.

That closes an important loop for Mission Control. A studio signal can move from shipped work, to review, to public distribution without disappearing into a separate planning tool. The operating surface now connects the work to the signal it produces.
